relationships.functionalForm: conditional; misalignment can reduce sleep opportunity and quality
relationships.moderatorsConditions: work schedule; light exposure; chronotype
relationships.evidenceNotes: Circadian misalignment and sleep restriction commonly co-occur; isolate effects where possible.

relationships.functionalForm: dose-responsive with floor and recovery effects
relationships.moderatorsConditions: task duration; circadian phase; stimulant use
relationships.evidenceNotes: Less sleep generally increases fatigue and performance instability.

relationships.functionalForm: conditional
relationships.moderatorsConditions: sleep disorder etiology; total sleep time
relationships.evidenceNotes: Fragmentation can reduce restorative sleep independent of time in bed.

relationships.functionalForm: nonlinear
relationships.moderatorsConditions: stressor controllability; appraisal; baseline state
relationships.evidenceNotes: Acute stress engages sympathetic and HPA processes.

relationships.functionalForm: cumulative
relationships.moderatorsConditions: stressor frequency; recovery opportunity; health
relationships.evidenceNotes: Slower or incomplete recovery contributes to cumulative dysregulation.

relationships.functionalForm: thresholded
relationships.moderatorsConditions: ambient heat; exertion; acclimatization
relationships.evidenceNotes: Lower hydration can increase physiological strain under heat and exertion.

relationships.functionalForm: thresholded
relationships.moderatorsConditions: altitude; exposure duration; acclimatization
relationships.evidenceNotes: Reduced oxygen availability can impair attention and increase effort/fatigue.

relationships.functionalForm: conditional
relationships.moderatorsConditions: pain meaning; controllability; medication
relationships.evidenceNotes: Acute pain commonly evokes autonomic activation.

relationships.functionalForm: bidirectional
relationships.moderatorsConditions: pain condition; medication; sleep disorder
relationships.evidenceNotes: Pain can fragment sleep, while poor sleep can amplify pain.

relationships.functionalForm: dose- and context-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: pathogen; cytokine pattern; age; prior health
relationships.evidenceNotes: Experimental immune activation supports an inflammation-to-sickness-behavior pathway.

relationships.functionalForm: thresholded
relationships.moderatorsConditions: exertion; cardiopulmonary reserve
relationships.evidenceNotes: Reduced oxygen transport can increase exertional fatigue.

relationships.functionalForm: thresholded
relationships.moderatorsConditions: inflammation; absorption; blood loss
relationships.evidenceNotes: Iron deficiency can reduce erythropoiesis and oxygen-carrying capacity.

relationships.functionalForm: thresholded
relationships.moderatorsConditions: diabetes; medication; adaptation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Clinically meaningful hypoglycemia impairs cognitive function.

relationships.functionalForm: dose-responsive
relationships.moderatorsConditions: tolerance; co-use; task
relationships.evidenceNotes: Acute alcohol effects impair motor and cognitive control.

relationships.functionalForm: dose-responsive
relationships.moderatorsConditions: age; half-life; co-medication
relationships.evidenceNotes: Sedative burden can reduce alertness and cognitive performance.

relationships.functionalForm: cumulative/interactive
relationships.moderatorsConditions: age; polypharmacy; dose; renal/hepatic function
relationships.evidenceNotes: Aggregate medication burden may impair attention, balance, or mobility.

relationships.functionalForm: time-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: dependence; abstinence duration; replacement therapy
relationships.evidenceNotes: Withdrawal can impair attention and increase irritability/fatigue.

relationships.functionalForm: time-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: habitual dose; abstinence duration
relationships.evidenceNotes: Withdrawal commonly produces fatigue and reduced alertness.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally monotonic but opportunity- and specificity-limited
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Behavioral specificity, attitude strength, perceived control, habits, and temporal alignment
relationships.evidenceNotes: More favorable behavior-specific evaluation usually supports stronger intention, but the edge does not imply action.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Valence, direct experience, accessibility, and opportunity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Stronger attitudes are generally more consequential for intention than weak or uncertain evaluations.

relationships.functionalForm: Expected-consequence integration
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Outcome valuation, probability, trust in evidence, and competing expectancies
relationships.evidenceNotes: Expected consequences contribute to evaluation according to their subjective value.

relationships.functionalForm: Valence-weighted integration
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Outcome expectancy, identity, moral obligation, and reference point
relationships.evidenceNotes: More positively valued expected outcomes generally support a more favorable attitude toward the action.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task difficulty, actual capability, opportunity, outcome value, and prior mastery
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater behavior-specific capability belief supports intention when the action is valued and feasible.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally monotonic
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Accuracy of perceived control, resource constraints, attitude, and norms
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater perceived control generally supports intention; direct behavioral effects require alignment with actual control.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold then saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Need for cognition, available capacity, time pressure, and identity relevance
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater perceived relevance normally increases issue-relevant processing when ability is adequate.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Threat severity, uncertainty, immediacy, controllability, and efficacy
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater perceived likelihood of an adverse outcome can intensify fear when severity and immediacy are meaningful.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Perceived likelihood, response efficacy, proximity, and personal relevance
relationships.evidenceNotes: More severe perceived consequences can increase fear, conditional on vulnerability and relevance.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold then saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Threat appraisal, self-efficacy, costs, and trust in recommendation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Believing the recommended response can work supports protective intention when the threat is relevant.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally monotonic
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Stressor controllability, resources, social support, and prior success
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater confidence in coping capacity can reduce expectations that action is futile.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Reference-group identification, norm visibility, behavior desirability, and actual opportunity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Believing that relevant others commonly perform a behavior can shift intention toward perceived typical action.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Anticipated sanction, legitimacy, identification, autonomy, and privacy
relationships.evidenceNotes: Perceived approval by relevant others can strengthen intention through anticipated social consequences or obligation.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Outcome favorability, prior trust, authority identity, and procedural visibility
relationships.evidenceNotes: Fair processes and treatment generally increase perceived rightfulness of the authority or decision.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Rule relevance, moral conviction, enforcement, costs, and alternative authorities
relationships.evidenceNotes: Legitimacy can increase voluntary intention to comply with a specified rule or request.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Support fit, relationship trust, stressor type, and actual access
relationships.evidenceNotes: Expected access to appropriate support can increase perceived ability to manage a stressor.

relationships.functionalForm: Stress-buffering / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Stressor intensity, support fit, controllability, and relationship quality
relationships.evidenceNotes: Perceived support can reduce appraised demand-resource imbalance, especially under high stress.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / time-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Exclusion duration, relationship value, attribution, and alternative groups
relationships.evidenceNotes: Perceived rejection acutely lowers felt belonging; longer responses vary between affiliation and withdrawal.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally monotonic
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Cultural meaning, task structure, competence, and relatedness
relationships.evidenceNotes: Experienced volition supports self-endorsed regulation and internalization.

relationships.functionalForm: Inverted-U
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Challenge-skill balance, feedback, autonomy, and task meaning
relationships.evidenceNotes: Feeling effective can support interest, particularly when challenge is meaningful and not overwhelming.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Feedback availability, goal commitment, and task complexity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Specific targets make comparison and progress monitoring easier than vague goals.

relationships.functionalForm: Inverted-U / feasibility threshold
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Self-efficacy, rewards, participation, feedback, and task complexity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Challenging goals can mobilize commitment when accepted and attainable; infeasible goals can reduce it.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Goal priority, resource scarcity, planning, and identity centrality
relationships.evidenceNotes: Incompatibility among active goals can weaken or destabilize intention for any one action.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Action versus omission framing, time horizon, perceived control, and outcome probability
relationships.evidenceNotes: Expected regret from not acting can strengthen preventive or goal-consistent intention.

relationships.functionalForm: Load-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task demand, worry, attentional control, arousal, and compensatory effort
relationships.evidenceNotes: Anxiety-related worry and threat monitoring consume resources and reduce available working memory on demanding tasks.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Appraised certainty/control, target relevance, domain, and regulation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Fear often promotes pessimistic risk appraisal and risk avoidance, but the effect is appraisal- and domain-specific.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Appraised certainty/control, target, accountability, and domain
relationships.evidenceNotes: Anger can increase optimistic risk appraisal and risk seeking relative to fear under studied conditions.

relationships.functionalForm: Capacity constrained
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task complexity, expertise, fatigue, modality, and strategy
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater concurrent processing demand leaves less capacity available for maintaining and manipulating task information.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Motivation, need for cognition, time pressure, and domain knowledge
relationships.evidenceNotes: Available capacity enables integration and issue-relevant thought but does not guarantee motivation to elaborate.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Perceived relevance, ability, time pressure, and accountability
relationships.evidenceNotes: People higher in need for cognition tend to engage more deeply when effortful thought is possible and relevant.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Attribution of ease, prior exposure, expectation, and stimulus type
relationships.evidenceNotes: Ease of processing can be misattributed to prior exposure and increase subjective familiarity.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Attribution, task expectations, accuracy feedback, and domain
relationships.evidenceNotes: Processing ease can increase confidence when interpreted as evidence of coherent or accurate thought.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / asymmetric
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Belief strength, moral conviction, accountability, involvement, and source credibility
relationships.evidenceNotes: Information that contradicts strong prior beliefs often elicits more counterarguing than congruent information.

relationships.functionalForm: Saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Context stability, repetition, goal consistency, and stress
relationships.evidenceNotes: Stronger context-linked habits generally show more automatic initiation, though the constructs are not identical.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold then saturating
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Cue specificity, competing responses, context stability, and inhibition
relationships.evidenceNotes: Stronger learned cue–response links increase rapid cue-driven activation of the response.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Goal activation, plan specificity, cue occurrence, and feasibility
relationships.evidenceNotes: Repeated or strongly encoded if–then planning increases accessibility of the critical cue and linked response.

relationships.functionalForm: Feedback-control / time-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Goal specificity, feedback accuracy, self-efficacy, and corrective options
relationships.evidenceNotes: Monitoring makes discrepancies detectable and supports corrective action that can reduce the gap over time.

relationships.functionalForm: Strategy- and timing-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Strategy, target, appraisal, intensity, social context, and goals
relationships.evidenceNotes: Effective regulation can reduce or redirect anger, but suppression and reappraisal have different effects.

relationships.functionalForm: Load-dependent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Anxiety, distraction, task demand, fatigue, and motivation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Goal-directed attention protects working memory from competing stimuli and worry.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Reward magnitude, stress, delay, domain, and current control capacity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Higher impulsive tendencies are associated with greater weighting of immediate outcomes, but measures overlap imperfectly.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Reward probability, deprivation, identity, effort cost, and context
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater reward sensitivity amplifies activation to reward cues and supports approach motivation.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Threat ambiguity, control, prior learning, and current stress
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater punishment sensitivity increases anxious apprehension under conflict or possible threat.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Situation severity, coping resources, social support, and current affect
relationships.evidenceNotes: Higher negative emotionality biases appraisal toward greater stress, without determining response in any specific situation.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Goal importance, task structure, role demands, and feedback availability
relationships.evidenceNotes: Conscientious tendencies support tracking and disciplined goal pursuit, but situation strength remains important.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Identity centrality, affirmation opportunities, source, accountability, and message framing
relationships.evidenceNotes: Threatening implications for global self-integrity can increase defensive counterarguing.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Group identification, efficacy, norms, status, and perceived intent
relationships.evidenceNotes: Threat to a valued identity can elicit anger and mobilize defense when the actor feels efficacious.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Importance of freedom, legitimacy, coercive language, alternatives, and trait reactance
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater perceived restriction of an important freedom increases state reactance.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Message strength, source, identity, available alternatives, and time
relationships.evidenceNotes: Reactance increases negative cognition and argument generation aimed at restoring choice.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Efficacy, identity, social norms, risk, and perceived obligation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Moralized positions often produce stronger commitment to associated goals and lower willingness to compromise.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Prior belief, argument strength, involvement, source identity, and ability to verify
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater perceived credibility usually increases the weight assigned to communicated claims when direct verification is costly.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Elaboration depth, prior belief, source credibility, and counterarguing
relationships.evidenceNotes: Arguments judged strong increase confidence in their conclusions when they are processed and not effectively rebutted.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Counterargument quality, prior belief, source, and opportunity for rebuttal
relationships.evidenceNotes: Strong counterarguing reduces confidence in the message conclusion, while sometimes increasing confidence in the prior belief.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Forewarning specificity, prior attitude, issue importance, message delay, and cognitive capacity
relationships.evidenceNotes: Motivation to resist increases rehearsal and generation of counterarguments when ability permits.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Source track record, argument content, relationship, prior belief, and verification cost
relationships.evidenceNotes: Epistemic trust increases willingness to update from socially communicated information.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / premature stopping
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Accountability, urgency, information quality, uncertainty, and alternatives
relationships.evidenceNotes: High need for closure can lower the subjective threshold for declaring available information sufficient.

relationships.functionalForm: Threshold / contingent
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Threat severity, control, reassurance, coping capacity, and time horizon
relationships.evidenceNotes: Greater intolerance of uncertainty increases anxious apprehension when outcomes are unclear.

relationships.functionalForm: Visibility can strengthen movement toward the observed group pattern; effects may reverse when the behavior is undesirable or identity-incongruent.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Reference-group relevance, baseline prevalence, public versus private response, approval signal, and credibility.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Visibility makes actual conduct available as social evidence, but it does not guarantee conformity and should not be treated as the prevalence itself.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually monotonic over the observed range, with saturation at high consensus.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Visibility, audience, relationship stakes, norm content, and cultural display rules.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Widespread public approval generally increases the chance that aligned conduct receives positive social response.

relationships.functionalForm: Greater approval of a standard can increase enforcement against specified violations; thresholds are common.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Consensus, legitimacy, group identification, observability, and sanction cost.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The edge applies to violations of the approved standard, not to behavior generically.

relationships.functionalForm: Typically positive for the sanctioned-against alternative and negative for the violation, with possible crowding-out or reactance.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Sanction legitimacy, severity, detection, identity, alternatives, and intrinsic motivation.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Peer punishment can stabilize cooperation or conformity, but high or illegitimate sanctions can provoke evasion or resistance.

relationships.functionalForm: A positive trend predicts subsequent prevalence change when the trajectory is credible and sustained.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Current prevalence, reference group, trend duration, signal credibility, and external shocks.
relationships.evidenceNotes: This edge represents temporal continuation, not an assertion that communicating a trend always causes adoption.

relationships.functionalForm: Larger majorities can be unanimous or divided; the association depends on how the majority is defined.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Group size, response categories, visibility, and selection into the setting.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The variables are distinct and should be measured separately; this record prevents treating majority size as unanimity.

relationships.functionalForm: Near-deterministic inverse when dissent is defined within the same visible response set.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Response privacy, unexpressed disagreement, observation window, and whether abstention counts as dissent.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Visible unanimity reduces available dissent even when private disagreement persists.

relationships.functionalForm: Consistent minorities sustain an accessible alternative across occasions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Minority size, behavioral style, task, response privacy, and majority openness.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Consistency can maintain dissent availability without producing immediate public conversion.

relationships.functionalForm: More co-present peers generally create more opportunities for observing peer conduct, subject to activity and attention.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Episode duration, peer activity, communication mode, visibility, and task design.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Presence is an opportunity condition; actual exposure still requires observable behavior.

relationships.functionalForm: Exposure from higher-status models contributes more strongly to status- or influence-weighted exposure.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Network position, relevance of status domain, prestige versus dominance, and model credibility.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Status is one basis for influence weighting and is not interchangeable with centrality or similarity.

relationships.functionalForm: Often increasing with diminishing returns; closeness also selects and sustains interaction.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Relationship type, conflict, communication quality, life stage, and opportunity for contact.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The relation is bidirectionally selected and should not be interpreted as contact frequency alone producing closeness.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually positive when interaction is voluntary and constructive; prolonged conflict can reverse the relation.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Interaction quality, voluntariness, shared activity, conflict, and relationship type.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Time together is an opportunity for relational investment, not a direct measure of closeness.

relationships.functionalForm: Additional relational domains often stabilize ties, though role conflict can create nonlinear costs.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Valence of each tie layer, role conflict, substitutability, dependence, and organizational change.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Multiplexity can embed a tie across settings but should not be assumed uniformly beneficial.

relationships.functionalForm: Reciprocal ties generally persist more than one-sided ties, with possible thresholds.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Relationship type, opportunity, power asymmetry, conflict, and reporting symmetry.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Mutual recognition and exchange support stability while remaining distinct from closeness.

relationships.functionalForm: Often negative and dose dependent; conflict repair or high dependence may weaken the effect.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Relationship commitment, alternatives, power, repair, conflict type, and cultural norms.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Negative interactions can destabilize ties, but some relationships persist despite frequent conflict.

relationships.functionalForm: Closer relationships generally provide more emotional support, especially under need.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Support need, disclosure, reciprocity, provider capacity, stigma, and relationship quality.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Closeness increases support opportunity but does not guarantee well-matched or helpful support.

relationships.functionalForm: Increasing with diminishing returns; composition and provider capacity are more important than count alone.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Tie quality, support type, network redundancy, geography, stigma, and current burden on contacts.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Larger networks usually expand the pool of potential providers but do not equal received or perceived support.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally inverse, though breadth can coexist with low contact intensity or low closeness.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Role quality, contact frequency, network turnover, mobility, and measurement definition.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Integration breadth is one component of objective isolation rather than its exact inverse.

relationships.functionalForm: Availability increases the ceiling for received aid; receipt depends on need, request, and provider response.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Need–support match, help seeking, provider capacity, stigma, and reciprocity.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Available support and enacted support must remain separate.

relationships.functionalForm: Availability increases opportunity for emotional support, with substantial selection and matching effects.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Need, disclosure, relationship quality, provider skill, and culture.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Potential helpers can exist without support being requested or effectively provided.

relationships.functionalForm: Repeated or chronic exclusion can reduce active ties and participation; acute episodes may instead prompt reconnection.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Chronicity, alternative groups, mobility, coping response, power, and whether exclusion is contested.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Ostracism is an event exposure; objective isolation is a broader structural condition.

relationships.functionalForm: Often positive and stronger where conflict of interest and vulnerability are high.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Interaction horizon, communication, incentives, monitoring, group size, and alternatives.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Reliable conduct supports cooperation by reducing uncertainty; interpersonal trust remains a distinct Psychological appraisal.

relationships.functionalForm: Generally increasing when future reciprocity and reputation are possible, with threshold and equilibrium effects.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Discounting, partner choice, observability, group size, and enforcement.
relationships.evidenceNotes: A longer interaction horizon can support cooperation but does not eliminate exploitation or coordination failure.

relationships.functionalForm: Often negative and potentially cascading as contributors update expectations.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Monitoring, sanctions, contribution visibility, group identity, inequality, and exit options.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Free riding can erode contribution, but sanctioning and conditional cooperation may interrupt the decline.

relationships.functionalForm: Higher credible sanction probability usually reduces free riding, with possible nonlinear and crowding effects.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Sanction legitimacy, cost, severity, detection, communication, and retaliation risk.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Effects are conditional and do not imply that maximal punishment is optimal.

relationships.functionalForm: Greater credible reputation visibility generally supports cooperation through partner choice and indirect reciprocity.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Information accuracy, audience reach, gossip incentives, actor identifiability, and future interaction.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Visibility can also motivate strategic impression management or reputational attack.

relationships.functionalForm: Higher rank generally predicts more deference; received deference also reproduces rank.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Legitimacy, expertise relevance, culture, hierarchy stability, and task.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Rank and deference are empirically linked but remain conceptually distinct.

relationships.functionalForm: Directional control of valued resources tends to create dependence in the opposite direction.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Availability of alternatives, switching cost, resource value, formal protections, and coalition support.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The sign must be coded consistently so the controller is less dependent and the resource recipient more dependent.

relationships.functionalForm: Steeper hierarchies often concentrate speaking and decision influence, though expertise and facilitation can moderate.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Hierarchy legitimacy, task type, leader behavior, norms of voice, and accountability.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The effect is not universal; steep rank can coexist with deliberately equal participation.

relationships.functionalForm: Accepted guidance can increase alignment when authority articulates a shared goal; illegitimate authority can polarize.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Legitimacy, leader competence, preexisting goals, dissent, and formal authority.
relationships.evidenceNotes: This edge is provisional and should not be generalized to obedience or compliance.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually positive but not deterministic; sparse networks can contain highly clustered neighborhoods.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Network size, degree distribution, boundary, tie type, and weighted or directed definition.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Density and local clustering summarize different levels and must not be merged.

relationships.functionalForm: Attribute assortativity contributes to segregation when the attribute defines the focal groups.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Group sizes, opportunity structure, baseline mixing, network boundary, and category definition.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Assortativity and segregation require baseline-aware measures; observed similarity does not prove preference or influence.

relationships.functionalForm: Higher constraint generally accompanies fewer independent cross-cluster ties.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Community definition, tie direction, weighted ties, network boundary, and redundant bridges.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Constraint is actor-centered; cross-cluster prevalence can be actor- or network-level, so level alignment is required.

relationships.functionalForm: More ties spanning focal clusters generally reduce relational segregation.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Group size, within-cluster density, tie strength, boundary definition, and opportunity for mixing.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The relation can be weak if a small number of bridges do not change most members' exposure.

relationships.functionalForm: Clustering increases the chance that multiple connected neighbors provide reinforcing exposures.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Neighbor behavior prevalence, time window, adoption threshold, tie activity, and seeding.
relationships.evidenceNotes: High clustering supplies redundant reinforcement but may limit reach to new clusters.

relationships.functionalForm: More adopting neighbors generally increases the number of reinforcing sources, conditional on degree.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Degree, exposure timing, source independence, tie activity, and network missingness.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Proportion and count encode different exposure functions and should not be collapsed.

relationships.functionalForm: Exposure through central referents can increase adoption prevalence with network-dependent spillovers.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Referent selection, behavior type, tie strength, baseline norm, susceptibility, and intervention saturation.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Randomized network experiments support influence but effects remain behavior- and context-specific.

relationships.functionalForm: Larger groups often make individual input harder to distinguish unless work is explicitly tracked.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task divisibility, trace systems, role clarity, output visibility, and workflow.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Group size is an opportunity condition; identifiability can be engineered independently.

relationships.functionalForm: Absent explicit assignment, larger groups tend to diffuse responsibility across more actors.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Emergency danger, competence, direct requests, role assignment, and group cohesion.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Dangerous situations and cohesive groups can weaken or reverse average bystander effects.

relationships.functionalForm: Higher turnover generally disrupts shared history and cohesion, though removal of conflictual members can reverse the effect.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Turnover voluntariness, replacement quality, tenure, onboarding, task, and prior conflict.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Turnover and cohesion may also share causes such as leadership or performance problems.

relationships.functionalForm: Greater underlying viewpoint dispersion increases potential dissent when expression is safe and visible.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Response privacy, status hierarchy, psychological safety, sanctions, and facilitation.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Diverse private views do not guarantee publicly available dissent.

relationships.functionalForm: Visible alternatives can stimulate broader search and disclosure of unshared information.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Minority consistency, decision rule, leader openness, task demonstrability, and time pressure.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Dissent can improve information search but can also create conflict or delay.

relationships.functionalForm: More equal participation increases opportunities for distributed information to enter discussion.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Expertise distribution, information uniqueness, facilitation, group size, and time limits.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Equal time is not sufficient if members possess redundant or low-quality information.

relationships.functionalForm: Factionalization can reduce cross-faction participation and concentrate voice within dominant coalitions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Relative subgroup size, cross-cutting ties, leadership, conflict, and meeting structure.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Direction depends on whether subgroups provide voice to minorities or entrench exclusion.

relationships.functionalForm: Common knowledge increases convergence in expectations about others' awareness and likely action.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Signal publicness, group size, communication reliability, strategic risk, and prior conventions.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Shared information without mutual recognition may not produce the same coordination benefit.

relationships.functionalForm: More aligned goals generally increase cooperative contribution, with saturation when capacity or coordination is limiting.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Incentives, task interdependence, trust, resource scarcity, and implementation clarity.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Aligned stated goals do not guarantee action and can mask disagreement about means.

relationships.functionalForm: Shared capability beliefs support collective effort when goals are valued and opportunities exist.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Goal alignment, actual resources, prior success, identity, task difficulty, and leadership.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Collective efficacy is a shared belief and should not substitute for objective capability.

relationships.functionalForm: Identifiable contributions generally reduce undercontribution by increasing evaluation and accountability.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task meaningfulness, contribution necessity, group size, incentives, and culture.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Identifiability can also increase evaluation pressure and strategic effort allocation.

relationships.functionalForm: Clear role assignment concentrates responsibility for specified actions on identifiable members.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Role acceptance, staffing, emergencies, overlapping duties, and formal authority.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Clarity must be mutually understood and feasible; nominal assignment alone may not produce action.

relationships.functionalForm: Larger unassigned audiences generally disperse responsibility, with important danger and group-membership exceptions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Emergency severity, competence, direct request, group cohesion, and victim relationship.
relationships.evidenceNotes: This is a social opportunity condition, not the psychological diffusion-of-responsibility mechanism itself.

relationships.functionalForm: Greater identifiability makes peer answerability and consequence assignment more feasible.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Audience reach, evaluation criteria, power, anonymity norms, and trace reliability.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Identification does not itself create a fair or legitimate accountability process.

relationships.functionalForm: Public actions make behavior available to wider reputational audiences.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Audience size, actor identifiability, information persistence, credibility, and gossip transmission.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Publicness can increase reputation visibility without determining whether reputation becomes positive or negative.

relationships.functionalForm: More intensive monitoring raises detection and opportunity for peer sanction, often with saturation.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Violation visibility, sanction norms, monitoring accuracy, relationship closeness, and retaliation risk.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Monitoring is not equivalent to punishment; peers may observe without sanctioning.

relationships.functionalForm: Repeated contact creates opportunity for friendship, with strong selection and quality conditions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Contact quality, equal status, voluntariness, cooperation, institutional support, and prior prejudice.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Frequency is necessary for many friendships but low-quality or hostile contact may not help.

relationships.functionalForm: Constructive, voluntary, cooperative contact more often develops into cross-group friendship.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Contact frequency, equality, disclosure, shared goals, prior conflict, and opportunity beyond the setting.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Friendship and contact quality are distinct and may reciprocally reinforce one another.

relationships.functionalForm: More prevalent cross-group friendship increases between-group tie density under compatible tie definitions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Group size, friendship reciprocity, network boundary, and whether all cross-group ties or close ties are counted.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Friendship is a close-tie subset, while cross-group density may include weaker relations.

relationships.functionalForm: More zero-sum rivalry generally reduces cooperative and respectful contact quality.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Rules, shared superordinate goals, equal status, prior conflict, and resource scarcity.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Structured competition can coexist with respectful contact, so the edge is conditional rather than universal.

relationships.functionalForm: Mutual dependence can increase cooperation when gains are shared and credible, or intensify conflict when leverage is asymmetric.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Dependence symmetry, alternatives, trust, institutions, scarcity, and history of exchange.
relationships.evidenceNotes: The functional form depends on whether interdependence is positive-sum, coercive, or zero-sum.

relationships.functionalForm: More permeable boundaries generally permit more cross-group ties and memberships.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Geographic proximity, institutional barriers, stigma, group size, and opportunity structure.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Permeability enables but does not ensure cross-group relationships.

relationships.functionalForm: Larger status disparities can undermine equal participation and make contact less constructive.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Authority support, role design, dependence, legitimacy, cooperation, and local norms.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Equal status within the contact situation can mitigate broader status inequality.

relationships.functionalForm: Overlapping affiliations create additional opportunities and incentives for ties across a focal division.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Boundary salience, network opportunity, competing identities, institutional barriers, and conflict.
relationships.evidenceNotes: Cross-cutting memberships may bridge groups but can also expose members to competing demands.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually inverse but not perfectly redundant; tolerance can differ by domain.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Norm domain; threat; enforcement regime; subculture
relationships.evidenceNotes: Tightness is partly expressed through low tolerance of deviation, but the variables should remain separately measurable.

relationships.functionalForm: Cumulative and mutually reinforcing over repeated transmission.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Institutional reinforcement; generational turnover; counter-narratives
relationships.evidenceNotes: Entrenched norms generally make continuity expectations more legitimate and durable.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent and often stronger under collective threat.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Threat history; institutions; ecological constraint; elite framing
relationships.evidenceNotes: Security priorities may support tighter norms, but reverse causality and common causes are plausible.

relationships.functionalForm: Monotonic with saturation.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Generation; migration; institutional reinforcement; domain
relationships.evidenceNotes: Shared valuation of tradition can legitimate continuity expectations without guaranteeing practice retention.

relationships.functionalForm: Stronger deference can increase default epistemic weight assigned to recognized authority.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Expertise; legitimacy; domain; competing authorities
relationships.evidenceNotes: Formal office and perceived credibility remain distinct variables.

relationships.functionalForm: Often thresholded by public challenge or insult.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Audience; gender and role; status; remedy availability
relationships.evidenceNotes: Honor norms can make reputation defense obligatory without universally implying violence.

relationships.functionalForm: Contingent; stronger face concerns often favor indirect mitigation.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Relationship; power; urgency; genre; trust
relationships.evidenceNotes: Directness can also protect face through clarity in some settings.

relationships.functionalForm: Typically monotonic across status-differentiated interactions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Language structure; role; formality; age
relationships.evidenceNotes: Honorific use is a linguistic convention, not a direct measure of obedience.

relationships.functionalForm: Overlapping but distinguishable by referent and household versus lineage scope.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Residence pattern; inheritance; migration; welfare institutions
relationships.evidenceNotes: Kinship intensity should not be inferred from family size alone.

relationships.functionalForm: May generalize outward or remain bounded to family.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Moral community boundary; scarcity; institutions; religion
relationships.evidenceNotes: Strong family obligation does not automatically imply broad communal sharing.

relationships.functionalForm: Repeated parent-child transmission and continuity expectations reinforce one another.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Migration; schooling; media; language policy; family cohesion
relationships.evidenceNotes: Direction and strength vary across cultural domains.

relationships.functionalForm: Elder modeling and inherited-knowledge legitimacy can mutually reinforce.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Age structure; education; institutional expertise; technological change
relationships.evidenceNotes: Elder status and knowledge accuracy should not be conflated.

relationships.functionalForm: Repeated majority-weighted copying increases persistence when the majority signal is stable.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Network segregation; majority visibility; payoff information; innovation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Conformist transmission may stabilize maladaptive or beneficial variants.

relationships.functionalForm: Prestige valuation increases model weight; copied practices can reproduce prestige.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Domain relevance; model visibility; institutional status; credibility
relationships.evidenceNotes: Prestige is distinct from coercive dominance and actual network centrality.

relationships.functionalForm: Higher fidelity slows drift and supports continuity.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Variant complexity; teaching; media; incentives; network structure
relationships.evidenceNotes: High fidelity is not sufficient for persistence when adoption falls.

relationships.functionalForm: Accessible memories can increase narrative centrality when framed as grievance.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Commemoration; recent conflict; elite framing; counter-memory
relationships.evidenceNotes: Memory does not uniquely determine grievance interpretation.

relationships.functionalForm: Founding narratives often supply identity origins and obligations.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Narrative contestation; generation; institutional education
relationships.evidenceNotes: Some cultures maintain plural or conflicting founding narratives.

relationships.functionalForm: Heroic exemplars can sharpen prototypes of authentic or admirable membership.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Counterheroes; role relevance; media; education
relationships.evidenceNotes: Narrative admiration does not guarantee behavioral imitation.

relationships.functionalForm: Shared meaning makes boundary symbols more reliable coordination cues.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Context; artifact visibility; institutional use; countermobilization
relationships.evidenceNotes: The physical or informational artifact remains separate from its cultural meaning.

relationships.functionalForm: Canonical stories can stabilize causal and moral schemas through repetition.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Education; media diversity; direct experience; contradiction
relationships.evidenceNotes: Schemas can also select and reshape narratives.

relationships.functionalForm: Often monotonic but contingent on role and belief.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Voluntariness; authority; life stage; community membership
relationships.evidenceNotes: Significance and obligation should be measured separately.

relationships.functionalForm: Costs may deter participation or strengthen commitment signals.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Voluntariness; alternatives; coercion; identity; resources
relationships.evidenceNotes: Cost has no universal behavioral direction.

relationships.functionalForm: Repeated synchronized practice may reinforce shared expectations and memory.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Ritual meaning; frequency; coercion; group composition
relationships.evidenceNotes: Synchrony is not equivalent to cohesion or belief.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually monotonic with threshold effects.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Issue framing; identity; authority; symbolic concessions
relationships.evidenceNotes: Prevalence and prohibition strength remain distinct.

relationships.functionalForm: Moralization can make trade-offs taboo; taboo treatment can reinforce moralization.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Domain; authority; conflict; material stakes
relationships.evidenceNotes: Do not assume all moralized issues are sacred.

relationships.functionalForm: Contamination or purity concerns often support prohibitions.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Object or act; religious authority; health threat; symbolic meaning
relationships.evidenceNotes: Many taboos do not derive from purity concerns.

relationships.functionalForm: Restraint is one possible content of a stronger display rule.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Emotion category; relationship; power; setting
relationships.evidenceNotes: Display-rule strength and restraint content are not interchangeable.

relationships.functionalForm: Both concern arousal valuation but depend on distinct emotional and moral contexts.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Role; goal; conflict; status; emotion category
relationships.evidenceNotes: Do not infer anger legitimacy from positive ideal affect.

relationships.functionalForm: Public self-evaluation can reinforce face-preserving conduct.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Audience; reputation visibility; role; status
relationships.evidenceNotes: Shame and face are related but not identical constructs.

relationships.functionalForm: Attention to context increases availability of situational explanations.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Task; expertise; salience; language; education
relationships.evidenceNotes: Population task differences do not establish fixed individual styles.

relationships.functionalForm: Dialectical conventions can sustain multiple or changing schemas rather than one exclusive model.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Domain; contradiction salience; education; political polarization
relationships.evidenceNotes: The relation can reduce or increase consensus depending on how contradiction is managed.

relationships.functionalForm: Inherited knowledge legitimacy and continuity expectations mutually reinforce.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Expertise; institutional science; crisis; generational change
relationships.evidenceNotes: Traditional knowledge can coexist with scientific or experiential authority.

relationships.functionalForm: Concern for distant collective futures can support intergenerational transmission.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Resource security; institutional trust; migration; perceived threat
relationships.evidenceNotes: Future orientation may also favor innovation over preservation.

relationships.functionalForm: Usually inverse but domain- and theology-dependent.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Control opportunity; efficacy; ritual prescriptions; institutional trust
relationships.evidenceNotes: Fatalism does not imply passivity in all domains.

relationships.functionalForm: Related but separable; direct speech can still rely on implicit context.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Genre; relationship; urgency; shared knowledge
relationships.evidenceNotes: Do not collapse both into high-context/low-context culture.

relationships.functionalForm: Politeness may increase euphemistic avoidance in face-threatening domains.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Topic; relationship; power; taboo; medium
relationships.evidenceNotes: Euphemism can also arise from taboo, secrecy, or legal risk.

relationships.functionalForm: Often inverse in specified contexts, but silence can coexist with otherwise direct communication.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Authority; emotion; conflict; gender; genre
relationships.evidenceNotes: Silence has multiple culturally patterned meanings.

relationships.functionalForm: Identity narratives can sharpen or soften boundaries depending on content.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Narrative inclusivity; conflict; migration; institutions
relationships.evidenceNotes: Central identity need not be exclusionary.

relationships.functionalForm: Clear authentic-member prototypes can increase exclusion of ambiguous cases.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Prototype inclusivity; boundary permeability; power
relationships.evidenceNotes: Consensus can also support inclusive prototypes.

relationships.functionalForm: Often competing orientations but coexistence is possible by domain.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Policy domain; group status; migration history; threat
relationships.evidenceNotes: Treat as distinct cultural conditions rather than endpoints of one forced scale.

relationships.functionalForm: Dominant assimilation pressure can raise costs of minority heritage maintenance.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Institutional policy; discrimination; diaspora support; generation
relationships.evidenceNotes: Threatened communities may react with stronger continuity efforts.

relationships.functionalForm: Larger generational distance can weaken continuity, though conflict may produce retrenchment.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Family transmission; schooling; media; migration; power
relationships.evidenceNotes: Cohort difference is not proof of irreversible culture change.

relationships.functionalForm: Continuity expectations motivate parent-to-child teaching and practice.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Language policy; family resources; migration; child agency
relationships.evidenceNotes: Transmission opportunity and fidelity remain separate.

relationships.functionalForm: Highly salient symbols can make membership distinctions more behaviorally available.
relationships.moderatorsConditions: Intergroup conflict; context; symbol consensus; institutions
relationships.evidenceNotes: Symbol salience does not by itself make boundaries impermeable.
